note: Coverage says what kind of evidence exists for a behaviour in each setting: measured there, bounded by a model or a related test, or nothing. The playbook's steps are responses that NASA's pages document; the badges are this project's reading of the evidence. It is not a procedure and not operational advice.

cells.name: Oxygen-rich air at reduced pressure

items.quote: In the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.text: 8 test rows lie near 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia and 11 near 34% at 8.2 psia; none is a solid material and none was taken in partial gravity.

cells.name: Materials that pass the test on Earth

items.quote: is not conservative, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.quote: the 1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials as evidenced by the negative ∆O2%, by up to -5.75% oxygen
items.source: Olson and Ferkul, Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test, NTRS 20130010991

cells.name: Pure oxygen, combustibles uncontrolled

items.quote: Because of the pure oxygen atmosphere, the fire spread quickly, causing a rapid rise in temperature and pressure that led to the rupture of the Command Module pressure vessel
items.source: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance: Apollo 1 case study

items.text: No PSI test row lies near pure oxygen at 4.3 psia, today's suit atmosphere: 0 rows.

cells.name: Electrical arcing

items.quote: Although they couldn’t determine a specific source of ignition, investigators found evidence of arcing in several wires in the spacecraft near the environment control system
items.source: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance: Apollo 1 case study

cells.name: Overheated insulation

items.quote: the heaters were left on for an extended period and reached temperatures around 1000 degrees Fahrenheit, degrading the Teflon insulation
items.source: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance: Apollo 13 case study

items.text: The alarm lab's 'overheated wire' scenario is the same start seen from the sensors: carbon monoxide without flame.

cells.name: A device that makes oxygen

items.quote: the canister ignited, shooting a three-foot flame with sparks and bits of molten metal across the module and generating a large quantity of dense smoke
items.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

cells.name: Spread fed by the fans

items.quote: the characteristic gas velocity of the minimum in the curve is on the order of 10 cm/s and also corresponds to a maximum in the flame spread rate
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.text: BASS-II in PSI: 129 test rows, with oxygen at the start between 13.6% and 22.2%. The table records conditions and gas readings. It has no column saying whether each flame went out.

cells.name: Burning with no flow at all

items.quote: Contrary to published speculation, the microgravity flame burned in some tests for over 45 minutes before extinguishing from a lack of fuel
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.text: FLEX in PSI: 274 droplet tests. The column 'Test end' reads Extinction in 186, Disruption in 61, Completion in 27.

cells.name: Spread fed by gravity

items.text: Simple scaling puts the buoyant flow near a small flame in lunar gravity at about 6 to 11 cm/s: inside the range the guide calls most flammable. A bound from a formula, not a measurement.

items.quote: the burn lasts for over two and a half minutes
items.source: Ferkul et al., Lunar Combustion Investigation: Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket, NTRS 20250010653 (abstract)

items.text: Of 2,009 test rows in the 24 combustion records of PSI, 0 were taken in lunar or Martian gravity. 19 records are flight experiments in free fall and 5 are ground work.

cells.name: A cool flame after the visible one

items.quote: This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.text: In PSI: the Cool Flames Investigation lists 87 droplet tests (PSI-39); the gas-burner follow-up marks 7 of its 179 normal-flame rows 'yes' under 'Cool flame?' (PSI-159).

cells.name: Flames almost too weak to see

items.quote: producing the weakest flames ever burned (approximately 1 Watt) and some burning for over 40 minutes before the experiment timed out
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

cells.name: Smoke that never reaches the detector

items.text: In this site's transport model, in free fall with the fans off, the duct detector stays below its alarm level for the whole ten-minute run. A model result: relative units, prescribed flow.

cells.name: Toxic gases rise faster than heat

items.quote: Overall, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide
items.source: Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment, NTRS 20240002981 (abstract)

items.quote: Air Force pathologists concluded the astronauts perished from asphyxia from carbon monoxide and other toxic gases resulting from the fire
items.source: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance: Apollo 1 case study

cells.name: Smoke particles unlike those on Earth

items.quote: Fundamental research in microgravity highlighted the vastly different particulate size associated with flames in microgravity
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.text: Smoke-particle measurements in PSI: SAME, SAME-R and the dust test DAFT, all in free fall.

cells.name: Smoke goes where the air goes

items.text: Without buoyancy smoke does not rise; it follows the ventilation. The Two realities model shows the consequence for a detector in the return duct.

cells.name: Dust that looks like smoke

items.quote: can discriminate between combustion particles and extraneous matters such as dust
items.says: A detector first flown on the Shuttle
items.source: NASA Spinoff: Fire Detector (1978)

items.text: The alarm lab's dust scenario: two separated detectors at once, no combustion gas, no heat.

cells.name: A detector silenced by the response

items.text: Stopping the fans stops the air that carries smoke to a duct detector. In the alarm lab the alarm latches, and the quiet detector is reported as 'smoke no longer reaches it', never as 'fire out'.

cells.name: Readings that cannot be trusted

items.text: Injected, replayed and clock-shifted readings (SPARTA EX-0014.03, EX-0001.02, EX-0014.01) are rejected by signature, sequence and clock checks. In the test runs, six seeds for each of nine situations, no tampering lowered a fire alarm. Synthetic scenarios.

cells.name: Stopping the ventilation

items.quote: the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s
items.source: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA TM, NTRS 20210011385

items.quote: A fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off.
items.says: Listed in NASA's guide among the critical misconceptions about spacecraft fires
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

cells.name: A suppressant jet that feeds the flame

items.quote: The local jet entrains air and sustains the flame even when the ambient airflow is turned off
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

cells.name: A fire the extinguisher cannot starve

items.quote: The flame finally extinguished itself
items.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

items.text: That the canister supplied its own oxygen is our reading of what the device is.

cells.name: Smoke and gases that stay after the flame

items.quote: Over the next several hours, the station’s life support system cleared the smoke and life returned to normal aboard Mir
items.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

playbook.step: Detect it, and tell smoke from dust

documented.quote: The conditions on a spacecraft require rapid detection of fires with limited false alarms
documented.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

documented.quote: One of the achievements in this area is a new device that monitors particulates and chemical species simultaneously to better detect the onset of a fire
documented.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

playbook.why: Smoke and dust particles were measured in free fall (SAME, SAME-R, DAFT). In partial gravity smoke can also rise, which changes which detector sees it first. Nobody has measured that.
playbook.adds: One sensor alone cannot tell dust, a failed detector or bad data from smoke. A second kind of sign can: see the alarm lab.

documented.quote: The crew quickly donned oxygen masks
documented.says: What the crew did on Mir
documented.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

playbook.lunar_basis: Earth gravity and free fall only
playbook.why: In Apollo 1 and in the Saffire flights the gases, not the heat, were the hazard that grew fastest. Measured at Earth gravity and in free fall, nothing in between.

documented.quote: the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s
documented.source: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA TM, NTRS 20210011385

documented.quote: A fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off.
documented.says: Listed in NASA's guide as a critical misconception
documented.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

playbook.why: It starved the flame NASA tested in free fall, and solids burn most readily near ventilation speed. That supports stopping the air to slow a fire. NASA's guide lists the belief that this alone puts a fire out among its critical misconceptions. In lunar gravity buoyancy keeps air moving after the fans stop, and no test exists.
playbook.adds: A duct detector that goes quiet after the fans stop has lost its air supply, not necessarily its fire. A model result on this site.

playbook.step: Use the extinguisher, and mind where the jet goes

documented.quote: Korzun began dousing the flame with foam from a fire extinguisher
documented.says: What the crew did on Mir
documented.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

documented.quote: The first two of the planned nine water-mist portable fire extinguishers were sent to the ISS in December 2015 to replace CO2 units that are currently onboard
documented.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

documented.quote: current findings show that local application of suppressant is not adequate for flame extinguishment
documented.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

playbook.why: The evidence pulls both ways. Extinguishers are certified and were used; in BASS a local jet dragged air into the flame, and on Mir the flame outlasted three extinguishers. Suppressant tests in PSI are all in free fall.

documented.quote: The flame blocked the evacuation route to the Soyuz spacecraft docked at the aft end of Kvant-1
documented.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir
A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

playbook.why: A documented incident, not an experiment: on Mir the flame cut the crew off from one of two escape vehicles. For a surface habitat nothing comparable is on record.

playbook.step: Clear the air, and keep watching

documented.quote: The station’s life support systems cleared its atmosphere of the toxic smoke over several hours
documented.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

playbook.why: In the Saffire flights carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide rose more than temperature or pressure. A cool flame can keep reacting after the visible flame is gone: seen for large fuel droplets only, not for cabin materials.
